# Worksheet: immunity that does not last

**~45 minutes**

The session stepped an epidemic forward one day at a time, twice over: a
**deterministic map** that moves the expected number of people each step, and a
**stochastic chain** that draws a whole number from a binomial distribution
instead. Both burned through
the population once and stopped.

Here you add one transition (recovered people become susceptible again) and the
model stops being an outbreak and becomes a *disease that stays*. You will find
its endemic level, see how far the one-day step sits from the truth, and then
watch the stochastic version do something the map cannot: die out.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Parts A and B are the session.** **Part C** goes further if you get there; not
reaching it is completely fine. Worked solutions are posted at the end of each
day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

**Prefer sliders to typing?** The
[Pluto notebook](../../notebooks/chapters/02-discrete-time-models.jl) for this
chapter lets you drag $\delta t$ and the ensemble size and watch the map and the
chain separate. Either order is fine.

**Coming from R?**

| R | Julia | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `for (i in 1:10)` | `for i in 1:10 ... end` | no brackets, closed with `end` |
| `sapply(1:5, f)` | `[f(k) for k in 1:5]` | a comprehension builds a vector |
| `rbinom(1, n, prob)` | `rand(Binomial(n, prob))` | build the distribution, then draw |
| `m[2, ]` | `m[2, :]` | row 2 of a matrix, every column |

## Greek letters you can copy

`\gamma` followed by `Tab` gives `γ` at a Julia prompt, but that completion
often does not fire inside a Quarto file like this one. Copy what you need
from here, or insert it from the command palette with the Unicode Latex
extension described in [Setting up](../../setup.qmd#optional-extras).

| Symbol | Reads as | At a Julia prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `β` | beta | `\beta` then `Tab` |
| `γ` | gamma | `\gamma` then `Tab` |
| `δ` | delta | `\delta` then `Tab` |
| `ω` | omega | `\omega` then `Tab` |
| `₀` | subscript zero | `\_0` then `Tab` |

`δt` is two characters: `δ` followed by `t`.

A subscript is its own character too: `R₀` is `R` followed by `₀`.

Plain ASCII names work exactly as well if you prefer them.
:::

---

## Setup

This is the session's deterministic map, given back to you, plus the stepping
loop that drives it. Run it and check the peak looks familiar: the one-day map
put about 201 infectious people at the peak, and by two years the epidemic is
long over with nobody infectious.

Note the shape of `iterate_model`: it takes a `step` function and calls it
`nsteps` times, so the same loop will run every model in this worksheet.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-setup
using Distributions
using StableRNGs
using Statistics
using CairoMakie

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)

function sir_map_step(state, p, δt)
    S, I, R = state
    infection = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
    recovery  = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I
    return (S - infection, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery)
end

function iterate_model(step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; extra = ())
    traj = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, nsteps + 1)
    traj[:, 1] .= u0
    state = Tuple(float.(u0))
    for k in 1:nsteps
        state = step(state, p, δt, extra...)
        traj[:, k + 1] .= state
    end
    return traj
end

u0     = [990, 10, 0]
p      = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0, ω = 0.02)
δt     = 1.0
nsteps = 728          # two years, and exactly 104 whole weeks
ts     = 0:nsteps

sir_traj = iterate_model((s, p, dt) -> sir_map_step(s, p, dt), u0, p, δt, nsteps)

println("R₀ = ", p.β * p.c / p.γ)
println("peak infectious: ", round(maximum(sir_traj[2, :]), digits = 1))
println("infectious at two years: ", round(sir_traj[2, end], digits = 1))
```

The parameters now carry one extra field, `ω = 0.02`: the rate at which immunity
is lost, or a mean of $1/\omega = 50$ days of protection. Nothing in the setup
uses it yet.

---

## Part A — immunity that does not last (~15 min)

The session's model had two transitions. Add a third, running backwards:

| transition | who moves | per-step probability |
|---|---|---|
| infection | $S \to I$ | $1 - e^{-\beta c I_t \delta t / N}$ |
| recovery | $I \to R$ | $1 - e^{-\gamma \delta t}$ |
| **waning** | $R \to S$ | $1 - e^{-\omega \delta t}$ |

Each transition is a *rate* turned into a *proportion of one step* by the same
`rate_to_proportion` conversion, so the new one needs no new machinery, just
one more line, and two changes to the state update, because people leaving $R$
have to arrive somewhere:

$$
S_{t+1} = S_t - p_I S_t + p_W R_t, \qquad
R_{t+1} = R_t + p_R I_t - p_W R_t.
$$

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-a1
function sirs_map_step(state, p, δt)
    S, I, R = state
    infection = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
    recovery  = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I
    waning    = 0.0     # TODO: replace 0.0 — how many people lose immunity this step?
    # TODO: add `waning` to S and subtract it from R in the line below
    return (S - infection, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery)
end

sirs_traj = iterate_model((s, p, dt) -> sirs_map_step(s, p, dt), u0, p, δt, nsteps)

# Given: what the continuous-time theory predicts for the endemic state.
R₀ = p.β * p.c / p.γ
S_endemic = p.N / R₀
I_endemic = p.N * (1 - 1 / R₀) / (1 + p.γ / p.ω)

check("population still conserved",
      all(k -> isapprox(sum(sirs_traj[:, k]), p.N; atol = 1e-8), 1:nsteps+1))
check("immunity is waning", sirs_traj[1, end] > 300)
check("the disease is still circulating after two years", sirs_traj[2, end] > 10)
check("the model has settled down", abs(sirs_traj[2, end] - sirs_traj[2, end-28]) < 0.5)
check("prevalence lands within 30% of the analytic endemic level",
      isapprox(sirs_traj[2, end], I_endemic; rtol = 0.3))

(; S_at_two_years = round(sirs_traj[1, end]; digits = 1),
   I_at_two_years = round(sirs_traj[2, end]; digits = 1),
   S_endemic = round(S_endemic; digits = 1),
   I_endemic = round(I_endemic; digits = 1))
```

The two numbers the checks compare against are handed to you, not derived here.
Setting all three continuous-time flows to zero (as many people entering each
compartment as leaving it) gives an *endemic equilibrium*:

$$
\frac{S^\ast}{N} = \frac{1}{R_0}, \qquad
I^\ast = N\,\frac{1 - 1/R_0}{1 + \gamma/\omega},
$$

which is 500 susceptible and about 37 infectious for these parameters. Note that
$S^\ast$ depends only on $R_0$: the waning rate decides how many people are
infectious, not how many are susceptible.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A

```julia
waning = rate_to_proportion(p.ω, δt) * R
return (S - infection + waning, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery - waning)
```

`waning` is a *number of people*, like `infection` and `recovery`: the
conversion turns the rate `p.ω` into a proportion, and multiplying by `R` turns
that proportion into a count.

If the conservation check fails, you have added `waning` to $S$ without taking it
out of $R$. If the disease dies out anyway, `waning` is probably still `0.0`,
which leaves you with the session's SIR model.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch02-endemic
#| fig-cap: "Infectious compartment over two years under the deterministic map, with and without waning immunity. The dotted line is the endemic level predicted by continuous-time theory."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)",
           title = "One outbreak, or a disease that stays")
lines!(ax, ts, sir_traj[2, :]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "no waning (SIR)")
lines!(ax, ts, sirs_traj[2, :]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3,
       label = "waning immunity (SIRS)")
hlines!(ax, [I_endemic]; color = :black, linestyle = :dot,
        label = "analytic endemic level")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### A1. Interpret

- The first wave is nearly the same shape in both models (the peaks are 209 and
  201), and they part company properly only afterwards. Why does waning immunity
  make so little difference early on, and what decides when it starts to matter?
- After the wave, prevalence drops to a trough and then comes *back up* before
  settling. What is being refilled during the trough?
- The plateau sits above the dotted analytic line, at about 45 infectious people
  against a predicted 37, with susceptibles at 447 rather than 500. The theory is
  not wrong. What else is different between the two calculations?

> *Your answer here.*

### A2. Refine the step

The last question has a testable answer. The map is an approximation to a
continuous process that gets better as the step shrinks, so shrink it. The
horizon stays at two years and only $\delta t$ changes.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-a2
refinement = map([1.0, 0.5, 0.1]) do dt
    n = round(Int, nsteps / dt)
    traj = iterate_model((s, p, d) -> sirs_map_step(s, p, d), u0, p, dt, n)
    (δt = dt, S = round(traj[1, end]; digits = 1), I = round(traj[2, end]; digits = 1))
end

fine = iterate_model((s, p, d) -> sirs_map_step(s, p, d), u0, p, 0.1, 7280)

check("the refined map lands on the analytic susceptible level",
      isapprox(fine[1, end] / p.N, 1 / R₀; atol = 0.01))
check("the one-day step is several percent away from it",
      abs(sirs_traj[1, end] / p.N - 1 / R₀) > 0.03)

refinement
```

The session measured this convergence against the ODE at a fixed time and got
first order. The same error is showing up here in a quantity you would report. At $\delta t = 1$ the endemic prevalence sits 23% above the analytic
level, and the susceptible level 10% below it. Both are large enough to change
the answer you would give.

> *At $\delta t = 1$ day, is the discretisation error large or small compared with
> the other uncertainties in a model like this? Your answer here.*

---

## Part B — the same model with integer people (~15 min)

The map moves fractions of people: at the trough it held 19.3 infectious
individuals, and a quantity that shrinks by fractions approaches zero without
ever arriving. The stochastic chain replaces each of the three flows with a
binomial draw, so its counts are whole numbers and the disease can run out.

That changes what the model can say. The map has an endemic equilibrium and sits
on it forever. In the chain, $I = 0$ can be reached from any state and nothing
here brings the disease back, so every realisation fades out eventually; what
varies is how long it takes. What you measure below is how many realisations
survive two years, and the survivors hover near the map's endemic level rather
than settling on it.

The chain step is given. It is your Part A function with `rand(rng, Binomial(…))`
around each flow, run 100 times from 100 different seeds. Each run is called a
*realisation*, and your job is the summary: which realisations died out.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-b1
function sirs_chain_step(state, p, δt, rng)
    S, I, R = state
    Y = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, S), rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt)))
    Z = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, I), rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt)))
    W = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, R), rate_to_proportion(p.ω, δt)))
    return (S - Y + W, I + Y - Z, R + Z - W)
end

nsims = 100
chain_ens = [iterate_model(sirs_chain_step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; extra = (StableRNG(seed),))
             for seed in 1:nsims]
chain_I = reduce(hcat, (traj[2, :] for traj in chain_ens))
chain_mean_I = vec(mean(chain_I; dims = 2))

# TODO: replace `falses(nsims)` — true for each realisation in which I reached 0
died_out = falses(nsims)

check("every realisation conserves the population",
      all(traj -> all(k -> sum(traj[:, k]) == p.N, 1:nsteps+1), chain_ens))
check("and every compartment stays a whole number",
      all(traj -> all(isinteger, traj), chain_ens))
check("some realisations faded out", count(died_out) >= 3)
check("but not all of them", 0 < count(died_out) < nsims)
check("the ensemble mean tracks the map through the first wave",
      isapprox(maximum(chain_mean_I[1:80]), maximum(sirs_traj[2, 1:80]); rtol = 0.1))

(; fade_out_fraction = count(died_out) / nsims,
   chain_mean_at_two_years = round(chain_mean_I[end]; digits = 1),
   map_at_two_years = round(sirs_traj[2, end]; digits = 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B

```julia
died_out = [any(iszero, traj[2, :]) for traj in chain_ens]
```

`traj[2, :]` is the infectious compartment of one realisation across every step,
and `any(iszero, v)` asks whether that vector ever hit zero. The comprehension
does it once per realisation, giving one `true`/`false` per run.

`traj[2, end] == 0` gives the same answer in this particular model, because
$I = 0$ is absorbing: nothing here can reintroduce the disease once it is gone.
It stops agreeing the moment a model gains importation, so it is worth asking the
question you actually mean.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch02-chain
#| fig-cap: "One hundred stochastic SIRS realisations (thin grey), their ensemble mean (red), and the deterministic map (dashed black). Runs that reach zero infectious stay there."
fig2 = Figure(size = (720, 440))
ax2  = Axis(fig2[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)",
            title = "Persisting in most runs, faded out in some")
for j in 1:nsims
    lines!(ax2, ts, chain_I[:, j]; color = (:grey, 0.15), linewidth = 1)
end
lines!(ax2, ts, chain_mean_I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "chain mean")
lines!(ax2, ts, sirs_traj[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 3,
       label = "deterministic map")
axislegend(ax2; position = :rt)
fig2
```

### B1. Interpret

- Most of the fade-outs happen between days 57 and 101, not later. What is it
  about that window that makes the disease vulnerable?
- The ensemble mean settles a little *below* the map. Given that some runs are
  sitting at zero forever, is the mean describing a typical realisation?
- The map says the disease settles at an endemic level and stays. Which model can
  answer "what is the chance it is still here in five years?", and what does the
  other one give you instead?

> *Your answer here.*

### B2. Experiment

Extinction was possible because the trough held only a handful of people. That
suggests the answer depends on how big the population is: a bigger community
has a bigger trough. Each run below rescales $N$ and starts with 10 infectious
people, as before.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-b2
function fade_out_fraction(N, trials)
    p_N  = merge(p, (N = Float64(N),))
    u0_N = [N - 10, 10, 0]
    runs = (iterate_model(sirs_chain_step, u0_N, p_N, δt, nsteps;
                          extra = (StableRNG(1000 + k),)) for k in 1:trials)
    return count(traj -> any(iszero, traj[2, :]), runs) / trials
end

populations = Int[]     # TODO: fill this list — try N = 200, 1000, and 5000

fractions = [fade_out_fraction(N, 50) for N in populations]
for (N, f) in zip(populations, fractions)
    println("N = $N → the disease died out in $(round(100f; digits = 0))% of runs")
end

check("three population sizes tried", length(populations) == 3)
check("fade-out becomes rarer as the population grows", issorted(fractions; rev = true))
```

$R_0$ was 2 in every one of those runs. Two communities with the same disease and
the same contact patterns, and over two years the smaller one loses it every time
while the larger one almost never does. What does that mean for a national
elimination target?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part C — from prevalence to incident infections (optional)

*Start this only if you have finished Part B.*

Everything so far plotted $I_t$, the number of people infectious *right now*.
Surveillance data are usually not that. A weekly report counts **new cases**, and
new cases are a flow: the `infection` term inside the step, which the model
computes and then throws away.

What the model produces is *incident infections*, not reports. The two match only
if every infection is detected and notified straight away, which no real system
manages. Read the series below as an idealised case series. The observation-model
session is where the gap between infections and reports gets modelled.

One more convention before the code. An interval runs from one day to the next,
so a daily incidence number has to be labelled by one end or the other. Here each
value is labelled by the day the interval *starts*: `daily_cases[k]` covers day
$k-1$ to day $k$ and is reported as day $k-1$. Prevalence needs no such choice,
since it is read at an instant. So when you compare the two peaks, remember that
one is a label on an interval and the other is a point in time. The gap between
them tells you incidence turns over first; it is not an exact lag between two
comparable moments.

Discrete time is where this is easiest, because the step already has the shape of
a reporting interval. The loop below keeps each step's infections; you turn the
daily numbers into weekly totals.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch02-c1
function iterate_with_incidence(u0, p, δt, nsteps)
    traj = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, nsteps + 1)
    incidence = Vector{Float64}(undef, nsteps)
    state = Tuple(float.(u0))
    traj[:, 1] .= u0
    for k in 1:nsteps
        S, I, R = state
        incidence[k] = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
        state = sirs_map_step(state, p, δt)
        traj[:, k + 1] .= state
    end
    return traj, incidence
end

traj_c, daily_cases = iterate_with_incidence(u0, p, δt, nsteps)

nweeks = div(nsteps, 7)
weekly_cases = Float64[]

for w in 1:nweeks
    week = daily_cases[(7 * (w - 1) + 1):(7 * w)]   # the seven daily numbers of week w
    push!(weekly_cases, 0.0)                        # TODO: replace 0.0 — the week's total
end

check("one total per week, and every week has cases in it",
      length(weekly_cases) == nweeks && all(>(0), weekly_cases))
check("no cases lost in the aggregation",
      isapprox(sum(weekly_cases), sum(daily_cases); rtol = 1e-10))
check("incidence peaks before prevalence", argmax(daily_cases) < argmax(traj_c[2, :]))

(; total_cases = round(sum(daily_cases); digits = 0),
   cases_per_person = round(sum(daily_cases) / p.N; digits = 1),
   incidence_peak_day = argmax(daily_cases) - 1,
   prevalence_peak_day = argmax(traj_c[2, :]) - 1)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C

```julia
push!(weekly_cases, sum(week))
```

`week` is already the seven daily numbers (week 1 is `daily_cases[1:7]`, week 2
is `daily_cases[8:14]`), so all that is left is to add them up. Cases are counts,
so weeks aggregate by summing; a *prevalence* series would not, which is worth
keeping in mind whenever you aggregate a time series.

Once it works, the same thing as a one-liner, which is how you would more often
see it written:

```julia
weekly_cases = [sum(daily_cases[(7 * (w - 1) + 1):(7 * w)]) for w in 1:nweeks]
```
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch02-reporting
#| fig-cap: "Top: daily incident infections and prevalence over the first wave. Each incidence value covers a one-day interval and is labelled by the day that interval starts; prevalence is an instantaneous state read at each day. The busiest incidence interval starts on day 15 and prevalence peaks at day 19, so incidence turns over earlier. Bottom: the same epidemic as 104 weekly infection totals, the shape a case series arrives in."
fig3 = Figure(size = (720, 600))

ax3 = Axis(fig3[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "people",
           title = "New infections lead prevalence")
lines!(ax3, 0:120, traj_c[2, 1:121]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3,
       label = "prevalence I(t)")
lines!(ax3, 0:119, daily_cases[1:120]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "new infections per day")
vlines!(ax3, [argmax(daily_cases) - 1]; color = :firebrick, linestyle = :dot)
vlines!(ax3, [argmax(traj_c[2, :]) - 1]; color = :steelblue, linestyle = :dot)
axislegend(ax3; position = :rt)

ax4 = Axis(fig3[2, 1]; xlabel = "week", ylabel = "incident infections",
           title = "Two years of weekly totals")
isempty(weekly_cases) ||
    barplot!(ax4, 1:nweeks, weekly_cases; color = :seagreen, gap = 0.1)

fig3
```

### C1. Interpret

- The busiest daily interval starts on day 15, and prevalence peaks on day 19.
  Routine notifications track incidence rather than prevalence, so which of the
  two does a surveillance system usually follow, and what does that mean for
  judging whether an epidemic has turned?
- Over two years the model produces about 7.7 infections per person. Nothing is
  wrong with the arithmetic. Which assumption is doing that, and is 50 days of
  immunity a reasonable choice?
- The weekly totals settle at about 70 infections a week. Two years in, would you
  call this epidemic over?

> *Your answer here.*

::: {.callout-note}
These weekly totals are still model output, not data: no infection has been
missed, no infection episode has been counted twice, and nothing was reported
late. The
observation-model session is where those gaps get added on top of exactly this
kind of incidence series.
:::
